 Jaime Gray, acting area director for the Port of Chicago, warned holiday shoppers to be wary of potentially counterfeit items as they hunt for deals this year. Federal authorities seize millions of dollars’ worth of phony designer items every year at O’Hare International Airport. (Brian Hill/Daily Herald) 
 By Charles Keeshan | Daily Herald and Susan Sarkauskas | ssarkauskas@dailyherald.com | Daily Herald PUBLISHED: November 20, 2026 at 7:44 AM CST Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... With the price of seemingly everything on the rise these days, who could blame you for searching online for the best deals on holiday gifts, especially high-end, designer items?
 But be careful, federal authorities warn: You might be buying fake and possibly dangerous goods. And your money could end up supporting international organized crime groups, including human traffickers.
 “If the price is too good to be true, it probably is,” Jaime Gray, acting area director for the Port of Chicago, said earlier this week at the U.S. Customs and Border Protection office in Rosemont.
 Next to him were several tables full of counterfeit goods: shoes, purses, watches, headphones, clothing, vitamins, Botox and more – even a car air bag. All were seized in the last week by federal customs agents in the Chicago area.
 Every year, CBP agents stationed at O’Hare International Airport find millions of dollars of fake items among the more than $300 billion in legitimate goods that pass through the cargo facility annually. They’ve uncovered everything from counterfeit Rolex watches and Gucci handbags to phony sports memorabilia and prescription drugs.
 “Today, nearly every single item is counterfeited (by criminals),” Gray said.
 Counterfeit UGG and Air Jordan shoes were among the items on display this week as federal officials warned of phony items hitting the market ahead of the holiday shopping season. (Brian Hill/Daily Herald) 
 He points out that buying a knock-off watch or iPhone isn’t a victimless crime. Besides the millions in economic losses imposed on legitimate businesses, you might be buying something that can hurt you.
 Fake Beats headphones could have faulty wiring that sparks a fire. The fabric or “leather” of that look-alike Michael Kors bag may have been treated with formaldehyde. CBP has found pesticides in counterfeit perfumes, and who knows what’s to be found in bogus vitamins and supplements. Agents have even come across counterfeit contact lenses.
 “It boggles my mind that people will take the risk. I don’t understand that sometimes,” Gray said.
 According to the CBP, the sale of counterfeits often funds organized crime and terrorist groups, and is linked to drug, human and natural-resource trafficking. That purse may have been sewn by someone, even children, forced into unpaid labor, in unsafe working conditions.
 Even though counterfeiters are getting better, Gray said there are still some telltale signs of a fake – flimsy materials, colors that seem off, misspelled words on the product or its packaging. CBP officers are often trained by legitimate manufacturers on how to spot a phony.
 A counterfeit watch that U.S. Customs and Border Protection in Chicago recently seized was on display during a media event to warn consumers of bogus designer goods ahead of the holiday shopping season. (Brian Hill/Daily Herald) 
 “The thing about counterfeit items is, it’s an opportunistic crime,” Gray said. “They’re looking to bring these items in at a value and preying on people who are looking, in this economy, to save money.”
 On the defense
 A Chicago attorney who founded an organization that assists incarcerated people will lead the state’s new effort to close the resource gap between public defenders and prosecutors.
 The Illinois Supreme Court on Wednesday announced Jennifer Soble as the first State Public Defender, effective Jan. 1. Selected from a pool of 27 candidates, Soble currently serves as founder and executive director of the Illinois Prison Project, which offers legal representation for incarcerated individuals.
 “Given her credentials, the Court believes it made an excellent decision in selecting Ms. Soble as the initial State Public Defender,” Chief Justice P. Scott Neville said in Wednesday’s announcement.
 Jennifer Soble, executive director of the Illinois Prison Project, on Sept. 8, 2023. Soble has been chosen to be Illinois' first state trial-level public defender. (E. Jason Wambsgans/Chicago Tribune) 
 The new office was created by state lawmakers to help ease the caseloads of county public defenders, particularly in rural areas where they’re often few and far between. Soble’s task, according to the Supreme Court, will be to work closely with the judiciary, public defenders and other justice system stakeholders to ensure uniform indigent defense across Illinois.
 “Over my past seven years with the Illinois Prison Project, I have worked with a dedicated team of lawyers, paralegals, social workers and advocates to free 220 people from prison, saving them nearly 4,000 years of combined incarceration and taxpayers roughly $400 million,” Soble said in the announcement. “I am grateful for the singular opportunity to bring resources, support, and innovations to the zealous advocates protecting the rights of indigent people statewide.”
 Before founding the Illinois Prison Project, Soble worked as a public defender and criminal defense attorney. She earned her bachelor’s degree from the University of Michigan and her law degree from Yale Law School.
 Loan scams on the rise
 Fueled in part by AI, personal loan scams are up more than 500% in just the past three years, a new report from the Better Business Bureau states.
 According to the findings, the BBB ScamTracker received 1,431 reports of personal loan scams in 2024. Just through October this year, the agency has lodged 8,673 such complaints, the report states.
 “In that time frame, artificial intelligence appears to have supercharged these scams as the public is inundated with multiple calls a day,” said Steve J. Bernas, Better Business Bureau president and CEO.
 Overall, the organization has tracked 16,190 complaints since 2024, with a median loss of $972 per instance.
 The scams often involve unsolicited calls or texts about personal loan offers.
 What are some red flags, according to the BBB?
 • Suspicious language around pre-approval. Scammers will try to entice you with “easy” money that can be in your account quickly.
 • Multiple numbers calling about the same loan. Scammers can change their phone number often to appear more legitimate.
 • Upfront costs to finish loan approval. By convincing their targets that they need to pay a fee for the loan, fraudsters steal hundreds and sometimes thousands of dollars.
 To avoid falling victim, experts suggest you ignore unexpected loan offers, seek loans in person rather than by phone or online, and do your research and take your time when considering a loan.
